title: Google Photos Unveils Customizable Redesign for ‘Collections’ Tab, Boosting User Control
body:
Google Photos is receiving its most significant visual overhaul in years, as the Android app begins to roll out a customizable redesign of the long‑standing “Collections” tab. The update, which follows the earlier introduction of a floating navigation bar, replaces the static 2 × 2 grid layout with a flexible, user‑controlled arrangement that lets people prioritize the albums, memories and shared items they use most. Early testers report a cleaner look and quicker access to favorite content, signalling Google’s intent to keep the photo‑management service competitive amid rising expectations for personalization and AI‑driven organization.

The revamped Collections view departs from the one‑size‑fits‑all approach that has defined Google Photos since its inception. Previously, the tab displayed a fixed set of cards—such as “People,” “Places,” “Things,” and “Recent”—in a uniform grid, regardless of how often a user engaged with each category. The new design introduces a drag‑and‑drop interface that lets users rearrange these cards, add shortcuts to specific albums, and even hide sections they rarely use. Google describes the change as “personalized at the surface level,” allowing the app to adapt to individual habits without sacrificing the underlying machine‑learning algorithms that automatically sort and suggest photos.

Industry analysts see the move as part of a broader trend toward modular UI experiences in mobile apps. “Consumers now expect their digital tools to reflect their personal workflows,” says Priya Nair, a senior analyst at TechInsights. “By giving users direct control over the layout, Google is addressing both aesthetic preferences and functional efficiency, which can improve daily engagement metrics.” The shift also mirrors similar updates in competing services like Apple Photos, which recently added customizable “Memories” widgets, and Microsoft’s OneDrive, which has been experimenting with user‑driven album organization. In a crowded market where AI‑generated suggestions are becoming commonplace, the ability to manually curate the front‑page experience may become a differentiator.

Behind the visual changes, Google is leveraging its extensive AI infrastructure to maintain the app’s smart features. The underlying “Lens” and “Search” capabilities—face recognition, object detection, and location tagging—remain intact, ensuring that the app continues to surface relevant content automatically. However, the redesign offers a more transparent bridge between algorithmic suggestions and human choice. Users can now pin a particular “Trip 2024” album to the top of the Collections tab, while still receiving AI‑driven prompts for forgotten moments, such as “Photos from your beach day last summer.” This hybrid approach aims to satisfy power users who crave control without alienating casual users who rely on Google’s automated organization.

The rollout is being phased in over the next few weeks, with the update currently available to a subset of Android devices running the latest OS version. Early adopters have praised the smoother navigation and the ability to collapse rarely used sections, noting a noticeable reduction in scrolling time. Some users, however, have expressed concerns about the learning curve associated with the new drag‑and‑drop mechanics, especially older users accustomed to the static layout. Google has responded by including an in‑app tutorial and a “reset to default” option, allowing anyone to revert to the classic grid if desired.

Looking ahead, the customizable Collections tab may serve as a testing ground for deeper personalization across Google’s ecosystem. Experts speculate that future updates could integrate cross‑service shortcuts—such as quick links to shared Google Drive folders or upcoming Google Maps itineraries—directly within the photo interface. As AI continues to refine how images are categorized and retrieved, giving users a tangible way to shape their visual dashboard could enhance both satisfaction and retention. For now, the redesign marks a decisive step toward a more user‑centric Google Photos, one that balances powerful automation with the simple pleasure of arranging memories the way each individual prefers.
